I step inside and put the register copy straight into Lord Edric's hands, then stay between him and Hale. "My lord, read this first. Your grandsire Aldous married Maud Fenn, a miller's daughter, in your own chapel, and Brother Osric will swear to it before Dame Crowe. The land is yours by plain deed, and the Aldermere line was Corvin's invention."

I turn to Hale with a bright smile. "And while you read, my lord, ask your steward why he wanted the book in my psalter, and why a man who 'merely attends' brought a hedge-carpenter named Garrow from Marrowford."

input.add_to_description: Day 2, ~6:30 PM: Wren's Persuasion (22) turned Lord Edric against him. Edric read the register copy, accepted that the land is his by plain deed, and ordered Hale confined to his room under guard, his keys surrendered, pending Dame Crowe. Hale submitted calmly, saying only that "Master Tallowmere will not be pleased." Garrow slipped away from the manor in the confusion.

Day 2 evening: Lord Edric knows the truth and has confined Hale. Plan: confess the false descent to Dame Crowe with Osric's attestation, keep the land by plain deed. Hale hinted Corvin will not be pleased; Garrow escaped, probably to warn Corvin upriver.

entries.text:
You step between them and press the copy into Lord Edric's hands. Your Persuasion check was a 22.

He reads it by the fire, lips moving at Maud Fenn's name. Slowly his shoulders drop, not in despair but in something like relief. "A miller's daughter," he says. "My grandmother. I remember her hands, flour in the creases." He looks up, and for the first time he looks his age and not his fear. "I'd rather be the grandson of Maud Fenn than the heir of a lie."

Then he turns to Hale, and his thin voice hardens. "Why did you want that book? Why did you bring a carpenter from Marrowford?"

Hale opens his mouth, and for once he has no smile ready. "My lord, I have served this house..."

"Give me your keys." Lord Edric holds out a trembling hand. Two guards are summoned from the yard, and Hale yields the keys, the copy of the chest key among them. He walks out between the guards with his composure intact. At the door he glances back at you and says, softly, "Master Tallowmere will not be pleased, mistress." Then he is gone.

Garrow has vanished from the manor, probably running to warn Corvin upriver.

Lord Edric sits, the register copy in his lap. "We will tell Dame Crowe everything, with Osric beside us. I may lose the precedence and the tax-right, but I will keep my land and my name." He looks at you with wet eyes. "You've given me more than Corvin ever did. Stay under my roof tonight, child. You'll have a bed, a hot supper, and my thanks."

It's nearly seven. The assessor arrives at noon the day after tomorrow, and Corvin may soon know where you are.

entries.text:
Lord Edric takes the sheet in shaking hands and reads it twice, his lips moving over *Maud Fenn, miller's daughter*. When he looks up, something in his face has loosened. "A miller's daughter," he whispers. "My grandmother. I remember her flour-dusted hands." He laughs once, unsteadily. "And I have been afraid of this for thirty years."

Your Persuasion check was a 10, and it only half works. He believes the entry. He means to tell Dame Crowe the truth, and that is more than you hoped for. But when you turn him toward Hale, his courage wavers. Hale has kept his accounts, his letters and his secrets for twenty years.

Hale answers before you can press. "My lord, the carpenter is a day-labourer I hired for the harvest. The girl is clever, and she twists things. I have served this house faithfully." His voice is warm, wounded, and perfect.

Lord Edric rubs his eyes. "Hale, you will keep to your rooms until the assessor comes. Tobin will bring your meals. We'll sort this when I have slept." It isn't a dismissal, but it's a leash. Hale bows, says "Of course, my lord," and goes, with Garrow trailing behind, and neither looks back at you.

Outside the window, dusk is thickening. Lord Edric asks you to stay in the manor tonight, in the guest chamber above the gatehouse, and tomorrow to help him prepare his confession. The assessor arrives at noon the day after.

Lord Edric reads the page once, then again, slowly. When he lowers it his hands are shaking, and not with fear. "Maud Fenn," he says. "Grandmother Maud. I remember her pies." He laughs, a cracked, astonished sound, and wipes his eyes with an inky cuff. Your Persuasion check was a 23, and it carries him the whole way.

Then he turns to his steward. Hale is ready, as you expected. "My lord, I only wished to spare you scandal. As for the carpenter, I hired him once for the stables and know nothing more of him. The girl is clever, and clever girls see plots everywhere." His Deception was a 17, smooth enough that Lord Edric hesitates.

But the hesitation doesn't save him. "Perhaps," Edric says, quieter than you've heard him. "But you wanted the book, and you wanted it quietly. Give me the spare key, Hale." A long pause, then a small key passes from the steward's fingers into the lord's. Lord Edric calls for the grey-whiskered gate guard, and Hale is to keep to his rooms until the assessor has come and gone. Hale bows with perfect composure. At the door he glances back at you, still smiling.

"Corvin will be disappointed," he says gently, and goes.

Tobin sags against the wall. Garrow is nowhere to be found; he slipped out in the confusion. Lord Edric sits on the edge of his desk and looks at you as though you were something he had thought lost long ago. "Stay under my roof, child. Whatever you want. Tell me how this is to be done, so that Dame Crowe finds an honest house."

"Maud Fenn," he whispers. "My grandmother. They said she was a miller's girl, and my father never spoke of it." A laugh breaks out of him, wet and astonished. "The land was mine all along."

Lord Edric takes your hands. He tells you he will confess the false descent to Dame Crowe himself, with Brother Osric beside him, and rest his claim on the old grant. "Better a plain lord than a false one." He offers you a bed in the manor, a supper, and, when you wave off payment, a purse of ten silver crowns as thanks. He asks only that you stay until the assessor comes.

Lord Edric takes the paper with shaking hands and reads it twice, his lips moving over *Aldous Verrel* and *Maud Fenn, miller's daughter*. Your Persuasion check was a 19. When he looks up, the fear in his face has turned to something raw and almost relieved.

input.add_to_description: Day 3 evening: keeper Marta Pell welcomed Wren free under Shelter of the Faithful. Corvin's wagon stopped here about three in the afternoon: driver and brown-coated Garrow only, watered horses, bought lamp oil, asked the road to Ashby Weir, and Garrow left a silver with Marta "for when a girl with a lute comes, tell her the master waits at the Ashby ferry-house." Marta distrusted him and says so. The wagon went on toward Ashby Weir; she thinks they'd sleep at the ferry-house, a long evening's drive ahead.
Day 3 evening: Garrow left word at Lantern's Rest that "the master waits at the Ashby ferry-house", likely a trap or a summons. Corvin himself is apparently ahead at Ashby Weir.

entries.text:
The woman's face opens like a shutter when she sees the brass in your palm. "Marta Pell, keeper here, and no one's ever 'Mother' to me but my own lads." She takes Biscuit's rein herself. "Bed, bread and a light, the board says, and the board doesn't lie. Come in, child. Your faith pays for your supper." Under the Shelter of the Faithful, that is free.

She talks as she leads the mule to a lean-to. Yes, a wagon stopped, about three in the afternoon, with the shrine-lantern painted on its side. "Which I'd have blessed, except there was no blessing in the men." There were only two, a surly driver and a sharp-faced man in a brown coat. They watered the horses and bought a flask of lamp oil. They asked the road to Ashby Weir and said nothing of where they'd sleep. No master was aboard.

Then she lowers her voice. "The brown coat left a silver with me. Said if a girl with a lute came by, I was to tell her 'the master waits at the Ashby ferry-house.'" She sniffs. "A man who pays to be believed is lying about something. I didn't like it, and I'm telling you straight."

So Corvin is apparently ahead, or wants you to think so, and the message is waiting at the ferry-house, a trap or a summons. The wagon is a long evening ahead of you, and Ashby Weir is another day's ride.

Supper is turnip soup, brown bread and a hunk of sheep's cheese by the shrine hearth, with the brass lamp throwing rays across the rafters. The bunkroom is empty but for you. It's seven now, and the fire is warm.

Corvin waited here since the previous night under the guise of a pious "brother of the lamp", met the wagon and Garrow at about 3 PM, and left with them toward Ashby Weir. Marta says he left a sealed note for "a young woman with a lute and a crooked grin, if she comes asking."

Day 3: tall, silver-haired man in a grey travelling cloak; stayed at Lantern's Rest Day 2 night, joined the wagon at ~3 PM Day 3 and left for Ashby Weir. Left a sealed note at the shrine for Wren, so he expected her to follow.

entries.text:
The woman leans her rake against the wall and wipes her hands on her apron. She sees the brass lantern in your palm, and her whole face opens. "Marta Pell, keeper here. Come in, come in, a child of the Lantern is never turned from this door. Your mule can have the lean-to and a bucket of oats, and there's soup and bread on the hearth. No coin, it's the god's table."

Over the soup, in a bunkroom smelling of woodsmoke and wool, she answers your question freely, because she's proud of her guests.

"A shrine-wagon, aye, this afternoon, near three. A holy brother had been staying with us since last night. Tall, silver hair, a grey cloak, lovely voice. He said grace like a bishop. When the wagon came in with the lathered horse and that brown-coated fellow, the brother went white as milk, then calm as a pond. They watered the team and were off toward Ashby Weir inside the quarter hour." She lowers her voice. "The driver was frightened. The brown coat was shouting."

The note is in your hand. Corvin knew you would follow. Outside, the lamp on its pole burns steady, and the wagon is a few hours up the road.

input.add_to_description: Day 3 evening: Marta Pell says Corvin's wagon stopped here around noon; the brown-coated man and driver watered the horses and bought bread. Corvin was not with them but a tall man in a grey traveling cloak, hooded, rode alongside on a bay and paid for their bread. They asked the way to Ashby Weir and left quickly. Marta noticed the brown-coated man was nervous. She gives Wren free bed and bread.

entries.text:
The woman leans her rake against the fence and wipes her hands on her apron. When the lamplight catches the little brass lantern in your palm, her whole face softens. "Marta Pell, keeper here. Come in, come in, a lamp-bearer never sleeps unlit under this roof." She takes Biscuit's rein herself and calls a boy to water him.

Your Insight check was a 20, so you read her easily. She's honest, a little worried, and eager to talk. Yes, the wagon came through around noon. A lean man in a brown coat and a surly driver watered the horses and bought bread, and they were in a great hurry. Marta says the brown coat kept looking back down the road. They asked the way to Ashby Weir and left.

"But the master wasn't on the wagon," she adds. "A tall man in a grey traveling cloak rode beside it, hood up, on a bay horse. He paid for the bread with a silver coin and never said a word. Gave me a chill, though I couldn't say why. He had a storyteller's hands, long and graceful." She gives you a sidelong look. "Friend of yours?"

Inside it's warm and plain: a hearth, a long table, a bunkroom with a few straw pallets. You get a bowl of barley stew, a heel of bread, and a bunk, all free under the shelter your faith gives you. It's just past seven. The wagon is half a day ahead and Ashby Weir is another day's ride. Nobody else is lodging here tonight.

input.add_to_description: Day 3 evening: keeper Marta Pell welcomed Wren free under Shelter of the Faithful. Told her the shrine-wagon stopped about noon to water its team; the driver bought lamp oil, the brown-coated man asked sharply after a half-elf with a lute and said "she'll come up this road". They pushed on toward Ashby Weir, expecting to arrive late tonight. The man in brown left a message: if the girl comes, tell her Master Tallowmere will meet her at the Ashby ferry.

entries.text:
The woman sees the reliquary and her whole face softens. "Marta Pell, keeper here. Come in, child, come in. Any walker of the Lantern is welcome, and your mule too." She takes Biscuit's rein herself and leads him to a lean-to with a manger. Inside there's a bunk, a hearth, and a stew pot. The bread and a bowl of barley stew cost you nothing, which is the rule of the house and of your faith.

She answers your question while she ladles. "The shrine-wagon? Aye, about noon. The driver watered the team and bought lamp oil, and said little. The other one, the lean fellow in the brown coat, wasn't so quiet. He asked after a half-elf girl with a lute, and I told him I'd seen none." She sniffs. "I didn't like him. His smile sat on his face like a lid on a pot."

She lowers her voice and glances at the door. "He left a message, in case you came. He said, 'Tell her Master Tallowmere will meet her at the Ashby ferry.' I didn't promise to pass it on. But you asked, and I'll not lie to one carrying the lamp." They pushed on toward Ashby Weir, she thinks, and meant to be there late tonight. Corvin himself she never saw, only the wagon with its painted lantern, and she noted it was hung with the flame pointing the wrong way up. "A strange way to paint it, I thought."

So you have a name for the meeting place, and it feels like an invitation to a trap. It's just past seven, the bunk is warm, and the road to Ashby Weir lies ahead. The assessor reaches Thornhallow at noon tomorrow, with or without you.

input.description: Plump, grey-haired widow, lay-keeper of Lantern's Rest. Warm but shrewd. Saw the wagon stop at about noon: driver watered the team and bought bread, in a hurry. A brown-coated man (Garrow) rode ahead on a spent horse and asked after a half-elf girl with a lute, calling her a thief. Marta didn't like him and told him nothing. The driver said the wagon would make Ashby Weir by tomorrow night and that "the master would meet them at the ford." She will share this freely with a faithful traveller.

entries.text:
The woman leans her rake against the wall and looks at the little brass lantern in your palm. Her face softens. "Marta Pell, keeper here. Come in, child, you and your beast. The Bearer's light is free to any who carry it, and so is my pot." She waves a stable-lad over for Biscuit.

Under Shelter of the Faithful you get a bunk, a bowl of barley-and-leek stew, and a heel of bread, all without coin. While you eat by the hearth, Marta answers your question freely.

"Aye, a shrine-wagon came through about noon. Driver watered the team and bought bread, in a great hurry, and he wouldn't meet my eye. He said they'd make Ashby Weir by tomorrow night, and that 'the master would meet them at the ford.'" She sniffs. "Then a man in a brown coat on a spent horse, asking after a half-elf girl with a lute. Called her a thief. I didn't care for his manner, and I told him nothing."

She looks at you over the rim of her cup, not unkindly. "I'd guess you're the girl. I'll not ask if he was right."

So Corvin isn't with the wagon but will meet it at the ford near Ashby Weir. The wagon is hours ahead, and Garrow is ahead of it, with a night's rest and a fresh horse if he can get one. It's nearly seven on Day 3, and Dame Crowe arrives at Thornhallow tomorrow at noon.

input.add_to_description: Day 3 night: Marta says a road-priest, Sister Ione, died at Lantern's Rest ~14 years ago; Corvin was there and left with the lantern-case and a bundle. Her entry in the guest-book is in a looped hand, which Wren can compare to the parchment.

entries.text:
Your Persuasion check was a 23, and Marta needs no coaxing past the first spoonful of broth.

"A road-priest in a looped hand?" She sets down her cup. "Why, that's Sister Ione. She came in out of a winter storm fourteen years back, sick to the bone, and died in that very bunkroom. Master Tallowmere was here that night, the only other guest. He sat with her. I remember her writing in my guest-book before the end, all loops and long tails, and him bent close, as if she were telling him something." She frowns. "He left in the morning with her brass lantern-case, and a bundle in his arms I never saw open. He said he'd see them both to the right hands. I never thought to ask whose."

She brings you the guest-book, and there's the entry: *Sister Ione, of the Lantern road. Lit and unlit alike.* The loops are the ones Osric knew. They match the parchment in your reliquary as far as a worn memory can say.

Then you go out to look at the brass lamp over the door. Your Religion check was a natural 1. You fumble the pole, nearly drop the lamp, and spend several flustered minutes learning nothing from it at all, to Marta's cheerful laughter. It's only a lamp, as far as you can tell.

It's nearly eight. Marta wants her story, and Corvin's ford is two days off.

entries.text: time: 1 hour 30 minutes later: Day 3, 8:34 PM

Marta settles across the hearth from you, and your Persuasion check, a 21, opens her up like a tap. Her memory is long and fond.

"A road-priest with looped writing? That'd be Mother Idony. She walked this valley when I was a girl, and she's been dead these fifteen years, poor soul. Wrote the prettiest hand, all loops. She kept a brass lantern-case just like yours." Marta frowns, remembering. "The last time I saw her she had a little one on her hip, a half-elf mite, and young Corvin walking beside her, carrying her bag. I thought him her nephew. I never asked."

You go out with her to the door-lamp, and your Investigation check, a 17, finds what a casual glance wouldn't. It's the same make as your reliquary, with the same etched rays. Under the base, scratched small, is a ring of looped letters ending in an *I*. Marta says Corvin gave it years ago and called it "a dead woman's gift." He never said whose.

You owe her a story, and you tell one. She laughs and wipes her eyes, and bed comes easy. The reliquary on your pillow feels heavier than it did.

It's half past eight on Day 3. Idony may be tied to your birth, and Corvin knew it all along. Ashby Weir is a day's ride ahead, Corvin's meeting is dusk on Day 5, and the wagon has a head start.

input.description: Dead road-priest of the Lantern-Bearer, buried at Lantern's Rest. Her looped hand wrote the true blessing in Wren's reliquary; the lamp mark matches. Corvin says she died owing him a debt. Her connection to Wren is unknown.

You fold the note into the psalter beside the ledger pages and take the broth. It's hot and peppery, and Marta sits across from you, glad of company.

"The brass lantern-case?" She thinks, spoon in the air. "He never said where he got it, love, only once, years back, with wine in him: that it came from a road-priest who died owing him a debt. Sister Ysolde Venn, a lovely soul, walked this very road. She's buried out in my yard under a plain stone. Corvin pays for the flowers."

She lets you take the lamp down from its hook. Your Religion check was an 18. It's old brass, rays carved in the shutters, and it's not Corvin's showy kind of piece. Tilting it to the fire, you find a tiny looped mark scratched inside the base, with the same round, trailing hand as the lines on your parchment, as if the same pen made both. Whoever Sister Ysolde was, she made this lamp and wrote your blessing.

You pay for it as promised, with a story over the empty bowls. Marta wipes her eyes at the end and says nothing for a while. Outside, the stars are out, and past the window a plain stone stands in the dark yard.

It's nearly eight on Day 3. The ford is two days off, the wagon is somewhere ahead, and Marta has the bunk ready.

She knew nothing of a looped-hand priest by name, but she remembers the first time Corvin came, about seventeen years ago. You tuck the note into the psalter and take the broth. Marta settles across from you, glad of company. Your Persuasion check was a 16, and she opens up like a hearth door.

"A looped hand? Why, that's Sister Ysolde," she says. "Ysolde Wick, who founded this place. She walked the Ashby road blessing travelers and died on it, twenty years back this autumn. Wrote the loveliest little blessings, all loops and flourishes. She carried a brass lantern-case just like yours, I'd swear to it." She turns her cup. "Master Tallowmere turned up a few weeks after she was buried. Said he'd been her friend. He took her few things 'to carry on her work,' and gave me that lamp over the door. I never thought to wonder."

You ask to see the lamp. She lifts it down for you. Your Investigation check was an 18. Under the base, scratched small, are the letters Y.W. and a tiny looped lantern, the same one etched on your reliquary's lid.

So the blessing in your lantern was most likely written by Ysolde, and Corvin took her case from her grave goods or her pack. Marta adds softly that Ysolde's grave is in the yard behind the shrine, under the pear tree.

Corvin's note says the parchment isn't his and that he let you carry it. Why he'd kept it, and why he gave it to a girl he was raising, is still unanswered.

It's nearly eight. You've a bunk, a good supper, and a story you owe Marta. What does Wren do?

input.description: Road-priest of the Lantern-Bearer who wrote blessings in a looped hand. Travelled with Corvin, died of fever at Lantern's Rest about seven years ago and is buried behind the shrine. Her brass lantern-case, with her true blessing, became Wren's reliquary. Your Persuasion check was a 14. Marta sits across from you with her cup and her face goes soft and far away.

"Seven years back," she says. "He came with a young road-priest, a Sister Alis, thin as a rake and burning with fever. She wrote blessings in a looped hand, little curling things, you could pick them out anywhere. She died in the end bunk, three nights after they came. He sat by her the whole time, love. I never saw a man weep so." She nods toward the yard. "She's buried behind the shrine. He paid for the stone himself, and he has never once spoken of her since. Took her brass lantern-case away with him, and I thought, well, he wants a keepsake."

She lifts the lamp down from its hook and turns it over. Scratched into the base, small and neat, is a looped mark very like the loops in your parchment.

"I always thought it odd," Marta says quietly, "that he carried it about as a sham relic after that."

The broth has gone cool in your bowl. Sister Alis, the lamp's mark, and a parchment in a looped hand all point at one woman. Seven years ago you were about twelve, and you have no memory of any family.

You've learned this at half past seven on the third evening. Corvin's meeting is two days off, and the Thistlewoods lie ahead. You could look at the grave tonight, sleep, or go on.

entries.text: time: 1 hour 30 minutes later: Day 3, 8:34 PM

Your Persuasion check was a 14, and Marta warms to you like a hearth to dry wood. Over the broth she talks freely.

Corvin never said much about the lantern-case, only that it came to him from "an old road-priest who died on the Ashby road, years back," and that he could never bring himself to sell it, though he's sold nearly everything else. She says it with a puzzled little frown, as if she's only now noticing how unlike him that is.

A looped hand, she says, sounds like Brother Aldwin, who founded this shrine long before her time. She keeps his old blessing-book in a chest, and she'll gladly show you in the morning, when the light is better and her knees are less cross.

Your look at the lamp over the door was brief. Your Investigation check was a 7, and it's only plain brass, with nothing you can see to say otherwise. You hang it back on its hook.

Then you keep your promise and tell a story, a good one, to a hearth and an audience of Marta, a pair of drovers and a sleepy dog. It's eight-thirty by the time you finish and the applause dies. You have a bunk, a full belly, and a morning's lead on questions.

Tomorrow is Day 4, and Dame Crowe reaches Thornhallow at noon. Ashby Weir is a day's ride on. The ford meeting is on Day 5, at dusk.

She carries a brass lantern-shaped reliquary of the Lantern-Bearer, a gentle road-god of travelers and tale-tellers whom Corvin worshipped only as cover; it holds a curl of yellowed parchment in an unknown hand that may be a true blessing or another forgery. She does not know if Corvin has sent anyone after her. Her ideal: stories should be free, and truth is whatever people can be made to believe. Her bond: find the nobles Corvin cheated and decide whether to expose him or quietly fix what he did. Her flaw: she can't resist a secret, and she lies even when the truth would serve her better. She has 15 gp, a rapier, a dagger, leather armor, a lute, a diplomat's pack with blank paper and sealing wax, and was raised with no memory of her birth family. The hook: as she reaches the market square, she spots a caravan wagon with Corvin's painted shrine-lantern sigil parked at the edge of town, but no sign of Corvin. A frightened young page in a minor noble's livery is pressing a sealed letter into the hands of the wagon's driver, and the seal looks like one Wren has seen in the ledger. Something is happening that links her stolen ledger to a noble house, and it needs a quick-witted liar to either sort it out or be caught in it. Open on Wren in the square, with the choice of how to approach the wagon and the page, and a locked iron-bound strongbox on the wagon's tailboard that she itches to poke at.

features: Darkvision: You have superior vision in dark and dim conditions. You can see in dim light within 60 feet of you as if it were bright light, and in darkness as if it were dim light. You cannot discern color in darkness, only shades of gray.
Fey Ancestry: You have advantage on saving throws against being charmed, and magic cannot put you to sleep.
Skill Versatility: You gain proficiency in two skills of your choice.

Bardic Inspiration (d6): You can inspire others through stirring words or music. To do so, you use a bonus action on your turn to choose one creature other than yourself within 60 feet of you who can hear you. That creature gains one Bardic Inspiration die, a d6. Once within the next 10 minutes, the creature can roll the die and add the number rolled to one ability check, attack roll, or saving throw it makes. The creature can wait until after it rolls the d20 before deciding to use the Bardic Inspiration die, but must decide before the GM says whether the roll succeeds or fails. Once the Bardic Inspiration die is rolled, it is lost. A creature can have only one Bardic Inspiration die at a time. You can use this feature a number of times equal to your Charisma modifier (a minimum of once). You regain any expended uses when you finish a long rest.  Your Bardic Inspiration die changes when you reach certain levels in this class. The die becomes a d8 at 5th level, a d10 at 10th level, and a d12 at 15th level.

Shelter of the Faithful (Acolyte): As an acolyte, you command the respect of those who share your faith, and you can perform the religious ceremonies of your deity. You and your adventuring companions can expect to receive free healing and care at a temple, shrine, or other established presence of your faith, though you must provide any material components needed for spells. Those who share your religion will support you (but only you) at a modest lifestyle. You might also have ties to a specific temple dedicated to your chosen deity or pantheon, and you have a residence there. This could be the temple where you used to serve, if you remain on good terms with it, or a temple where you have found a new home. While near your temple, you can call upon the priests for assistance, provided the assistance you ask for is not hazardous and you remain in good standing with your temple.

line: I fold the note, tuck it into the psalter next to the ledger pages, and sit down to the broth with a calm face. "Mother Pell, you've known Corvin seven years. Did he ever mention who gave him the brass lantern-case, or a road-priest who wrote blessings in a looped hand? I'd also like a look at the lamp he gave you, if you'll let me, and I'll tell you a good story for it after supper."

input.add_to_description: Marta's memories (Day 3): seven years ago Corvin arrived with a small girl on his saddle and a brass lantern-case, and wept at the shrine, which Marta never saw him do before or since. He said the case "wasn't his to keep." The lamp over the door that he gave has a hidden maker's mark on its base: a looped initial "A" over a small lantern, the same loops as the parchment. The road-priest who made it is called Brother Anselm, long dead, who kept a way-shrine at Ashby Weir ford.

input.description: Long-dead road-priest of the Lantern-Bearer who kept a way-shrine at Ashby Weir ford. Likely wrote the blessing in Wren's reliquary; maker's mark is a looped "A" over a small lantern. Connection to Corvin and to Wren's lost birth family unknown.

Your Persuasion check was a 22, and Marta opens up like a woman who has waited years for someone to ask.

"Seven years ago," she says, ladling more broth. "He came in with a little girl asleep on his saddle, and a brass case in his hand. He wept at my shrine, love. In seven years of knowing him, that's the only time. He said the case 'wasn't his to keep,' and wouldn't say more." She looks at you for a long moment, and doesn't say what she's thinking.

Then she takes down the brass lamp from over the door and sets it on the table. On the underside of the base, half hidden by soot, is a tiny mark: a looped letter A over a small lantern. You've seen those loops. They are the hand of the parchment in your reliquary. "That's Brother Anselm's mark," Marta says. "A road-priest, dead many years. He kept the way-shrine at Ashby Weir ford. Corvin gave me this lamp the same week he wept."

The ford where Corvin wants to meet you is the same ford where Anselm kept his shrine.

You eat, and tell Marta a good story as promised, about a lantern that learned to walk. She laughs in the right places. It's eight o'clock now, the bunk is warm, and the road to Ashby Weir lies ahead. Corvin is a day ahead of you, with a team and a head start, but he has named the place and the time, and you have until dusk on Day 5.

What does Wren do?
